prompt: `go vet` is silent and `go test` passes, yet six runs of `pcount` over the same 20,000-line file print six different line counts. What is the likeliest explanation?
hint: The workers share one `Summary`.

choices.text: The log file is rewritten between one run and the next
choices.why: `access.log` was written once by `genlog` with a fixed seed; the input was identical every time.

choices.text: Lost increments on a shared counter
choices.why: Right. Two workers read the same old value of `s.Lines` and both write back one more; vet reads no timing and the four-line test hardly ever overlaps.

choices.text: `bufio.Scanner` drops lines when it reads fast
choices.why: The lines are read by one goroutine before any worker starts, and the fixed version counts 20,000 every time from the same reader.

choices.text: `go vet` reports every data race, so the fault is in the hardware
choices.why: `go vet` checks code shapes it recognises; a race depends on what happens at run time, which only `-race` watches.

prompt: In the race report, the frame under `sync.(*WaitGroup).Go()` is `checkParallel()` at `parallel_test.go:21`, which is the call to `CountParallel`. Where was `wg.Go` actually called?
hint: One frame is missing from that stack, and the lesson said why.

choices.text: In `checkParallel`, at line 21 of the test
choices.why: Line 21 calls `CountParallel`; the test never calls `wg.Go` itself.

choices.text: One level deeper, in the function line 21 calls; its frame is missing
choices.why: Right. The `sync` package is compiled without the entry and exit bookkeeping the detector builds stacks from, so `CountParallel`, the caller of `wg.Go`, drops out and the next frame is one level too high.

choices.text: In `testing.tRunner`, which starts every goroutine of a test
choices.why: `tRunner` starts the test function's goroutine, not the workers; the workers come from `wg.Go`.

choices.text: Nowhere: the goroutines were started by the runtime
choices.why: Every goroutine has a `go` statement somewhere; here it is inside `wg.Go`, called from `CountParallel`'s loop.

prompt: `./pcount-race < access.log 2>/dev/null; echo $?` printed a count and then an exit status, with every report thrown away. Which status, the race detector's default for a run that saw a race?
hint: The same number `go-concurrency` lesson 16 met at the end of every report.

prompt: Which of these changes to the first `CountParallel` remove the race on `s.Lines` and `s.Total`? Choose all that apply.
hint: A fix either orders the accesses or stops them sharing memory.

choices.text: Move `mu.Lock()` above `s.Lines++`
choices.why: Yes, this is the fix the lesson made: every access to `s` then happens under one lock, so each is ordered against the others.

choices.text: Give each worker a `Summary` of its own and add them up after `wg.Wait()`
choices.why: Yes. No two goroutines touch the same counters any more, and `wg.Wait()` orders every worker's writes before the sum.

choices.text: Run the tests with `-cpu 1`
choices.why: That changes what the run does, not the code: with explicit workers the race remains, and `pcount` still loses lines on a big machine.

choices.text: Set `GORACE=halt_on_error=1`
choices.why: It stops the run at the first report. The race is still in the code, and the binary without `-race` ignores `GORACE` entirely.

prompt: `TestCountParallelOneWorker` passed under `go test -race` while `CountParallel` still had its race. Why did the detector stay silent?
hint: Count the goroutines that touch `s`.

choices.text: One worker means one goroutine, and a race needs two
choices.why: Right. The detector reports two unordered accesses from different goroutines, and that run had only one goroutine doing the work.

choices.text: The detector samples accesses and missed these
choices.why: It checks every access the instrumented code makes; there was simply no second goroutine to collide with.

choices.text: Four lines are too few for the detector to start
choices.why: Section 02's test used the same four lines with two workers and failed every time.

choices.text: `-run OneWorker` turned the detector off for the other tests
choices.why: `-run` picks which tests run; the detector watches whatever runs.

prompt: `TestCountParallelDefault` passes with `-race` under `taskset -c 0` and fails without it on the same 4-CPU machine. What changed between the two runs?
hint: The test passes zero workers.

choices.text: `taskset` turns the detector off for pinned processes
choices.why: The detector ran in both; under `taskset -c 0` the other test with two workers still failed.

choices.text: `GOMAXPROCS` defaulted to 1, so zero meant a single worker
choices.why: Right. The default follows the affinity mask, so 'one per CPU' became one goroutine and the racy path never ran.

choices.text: One CPU is too slow for two accesses to overlap
choices.why: Overlap in time is not what the detector looks for; it looks for accesses that nothing ordered, and two goroutines on one CPU still produce them.

choices.text: The test cache answered for the pinned run
choices.why: Both commands used `-count=1`, which never answers from the cache.

prompt: A CI job runs in a container limited to one CPU on a 16-CPU host, with no `GOMAXPROCS` set. What does `runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0)` return under Go 1.27.1, according to its documentation?
hint: The quota is one input; the documentation names a floor.

choices.text: 16, because a container's quota is ignored
choices.why: The documentation lists the cgroup CPU quota among the inputs on Linux, since Go 1.25's default.

choices.text: 1, matching the quota
choices.why: The quota never brings the default below 2 unless the machine or the affinity mask has fewer than two CPUs.

choices.text: 2: a quota alone never takes it lower
choices.why: Right. So `CountParallel(r, 0)` starts two workers there, and the default test catches the race; a one-CPU VM or `taskset -c 0` would give 1.

choices.text: 0, until the program calls `runtime.GOMAXPROCS` with a value
choices.why: Called with 0 it reports the current setting, which always has a default of at least 1.

prompt: `go test -race ___ 1,4 ./...` runs every test twice, once with `GOMAXPROCS` set to 1 and once with it set to 4.
hint: A `go test` flag taking a list of values.

prompt: Pinned to one CPU with `taskset -c 0`, `TestCountParallel`, which asks for two workers, still failed with `-race`. What does that show?
hint: Compare it with the zero-worker test on the same CPU.

choices.text: The detector needs two goroutines, not two CPUs
choices.why: Right. Two goroutines taking turns on one CPU still make accesses that nothing orders, and that is all a report needs.

choices.text: `taskset` does not really restrict a Go program
choices.why: It did: `taskset -c 0 nproc` printed 1, and the zero-worker test ran a single worker.

choices.text: Races are more frequent on one CPU than on four
choices.why: The plain `pcount` lost lines on four CPUs; the detector's verdict does not depend on how often increments collide.

choices.text: The test failed for a reason other than the race
choices.why: Its failure was the race report on `s.Lines`, the same as on four CPUs.

prompt: With and without `-race`, `-benchmem` reported about 4,133,000 B/op for `BenchmarkCountParallel`, while the kernel's `VmHWM` read 19,748 kB and 46,020 kB. Why does `-benchmem` miss the difference?
hint: Ask what `-benchmem` counts.

choices.text: The detector allocated nothing in this benchmark
choices.why: The kernel saw the process more than double its peak; that memory came from somewhere.

choices.text: `-benchmem` turns the detector off while it measures
choices.why: The race run was 4.7 times slower, so the detector was clearly running.

choices.text: It counts the Go heap, and the detector's records live outside it
choices.why: Right. The detector's memory is taken by its own runtime, which the Go allocator's statistics never see; only the operating system's view shows it.

choices.text: `VmHWM` includes the size of the binary on disk
choices.why: `VmHWM` is resident memory at the peak; the binary grew by about 1.3 MB, far less than the 26 MB gap.

prompt: `BenchmarkCountParallel` took 10,830,468 ns/op plainly and 50,833,093 ns/op with `-race`. How many times as long is the race run, to one decimal place?
hint: Divide the second by the first.

prompt: The tests of `internal/tally` take 3 ms plainly and 1.017 s with `-race`, and 0.013 s with `GORACE=atexit_sleep_ms=0`. What is the extra second?
hint: It does not grow with the work the tests do.

choices.text: The time to compile the race build
choices.why: `go test` reports the run of the test binary, not its build; and the build was already cached.

choices.text: A one-second wait before a race-enabled program exits
choices.why: Right. The detector waits 1,000 ms at exit so that goroutines still running get a chance to be reported; setting it to 0 skips the wait.

choices.text: The instrumentation slowing every test by the same factor
choices.why: A slowdown by a factor would turn 3 ms into a few tens of milliseconds, not a second, and would not vanish with one variable.

choices.text: Writing the reports to standard error
choices.why: These tests passed and printed no report at all.

prompt: Match each line a `-race` run printed with its cause.
hint: Two are refusals before anything compiles.

pairs.left: `go: -race requires cgo; enable cgo by setting CGO_ENABLED=1`
pairs.right: cgo is off, by the variable or for want of a C compiler
no race runtime exists for that platform
the second the detector waits at exit
two goroutines touched memory with nothing ordering them

prompt: Why does the workflow's test step say `-count=1`?
hint: Two identical `go test -race ./...` runs in a row printed `(cached)` the second time.

choices.text: Without it, go test runs every test only once per package
choices.why: Once is the default anyway: `-count` says how many times, and 1 is what you get without it.

choices.text: It turns off the detector's exit sleep
choices.why: That is `GORACE=atexit_sleep_ms=0`; `-count` has nothing to do with the detector.

choices.text: A restored build cache would otherwise replay an old pass
choices.why: Right. setup-go restores the build cache by default, results of earlier passes live there, and `-count=1` is the documented way to make go test run anyway.

choices.text: GitHub Actions requires it for any step that sets `CGO_ENABLED`
choices.why: Actions knows nothing about go test's flags; the reason is go test's own cache.

prompt: Put the places a change passes through in order, from the first that runs the detector to the one that never does.
hint: From a pull request to what users run.
items: the push to `main`: the same tests, and `go build -race`
staging: the race build serves real traffic with `log_path` set
the release: a plain `go build`, with no detector

prompt: A pull request's race job fails with a report naming two lines of new code. A teammate reruns the job and it goes green. What should happen next?
hint: What does a green rerun tell you about the code?

choices.text: Merge: the second run proves the first was noise
choices.why: A report is two accesses the detector watched happen. A green rerun only shows a run that did not take that path with two goroutines.

choices.text: Mark the test as flaky so it stops blocking merges
choices.why: That test is what made the goroutines meet; disabling it removes the only witness.

choices.text: Fix the two lines or revert the change, then rerun
choices.why: Right. The report already names the lines; the fix goes through the same step, with `-count` and `-cpu`, and must come out clean.

choices.text: Add an automatic retry so a single bad run never fails the job
choices.why: That builds 'rerun until green' into the pipeline, and a race only shows on some runs.

prompt: On a staging machine, `GORACE=___=/var/log/pcount/race` makes each race-enabled process write its reports to `/var/log/pcount/race.` followed by its process id.
hint: The option is named after where the log goes.

prompt: Why should the CI test step leave `halt_on_error` at its default rather than set `GORACE=halt_on_error=1`?
hint: What happens to the tests after the first report?

choices.text: It makes the detector miss the first race
choices.why: It reports the first race and then stops; the first is never the one lost.

choices.text: It would stop at the first report and hide the rest
choices.why: Right. One report is easier to read by hand, but CI should show every race in one run, and the tests after the stop give no result at all.

choices.text: A halted run exits with status 0, so the job would go green
choices.why: A halted run still exits with the detector's status; the job fails either way.

choices.text: It works only together with `log_path`, which CI does not set
choices.why: The two options are independent; section 02 used `halt_on_error` alone.

prompt: To stop the race job blocking merges, somebody sets `GORACE=exitcode=0` on the step running `go test -race ./...`. What happens on the next pull request that brings a race?
hint: Who decides that a test failed?

choices.text: The job goes green, because every race now exits 0
choices.why: That would be true of a plain program like `pcount-race`, but not of a test binary.

choices.text: It still fails: the testing package fails the test
choices.why: Right. A test binary that sees a race fails with status 1 whatever `exitcode` says, so the setting changes nothing in that step, and only hides races where it is applied to a plain binary.

choices.text: go test refuses to run, because 0 is not a valid exit code
choices.why: 0 is accepted; the detector simply uses it for runs with a race.

choices.text: The detector stops writing reports
choices.why: `exitcode` changes only the status; the reports are written as before.

prompt: `go test -race -count=3 -cpu 1,2,4 ./...` ran after the fix. How many times did it run `TestCountParallelDefault`?
hint: `-count` applies once per value of `-cpu`.
